speaker: Sofia
text: Wei! You're back. How was Lisbon?

speaker: Wei
text: Amazing, but I'm still on Lisbon time, so if I say something dumb, that's why.

speaker: Grace
text: OK, let's get into it, we've got half an hour. Today is about getting the product search index off the nightly batch job. Right now the Airflow job rebuilds the whole Elasticsearch index from the catalog database every night, so prices and stock in search can be up to a day stale.

speaker: Hamid
text: And that's costing us. Last flash sale we had people adding items to the cart at the old price, and we sold stuff that was already out of stock. What I need is price and stock changes showing up in search within a minute. That's the number.

speaker: Grace
text: And ranking stays as it is. Nobody touches relevance or personalization as part of this project.

speaker: Hamid
text: Correct, ranking is out of scope.

speaker: Olumide
text: Some numbers for context. We've got about forty million SKUs. The nightly rebuild takes around five hours now. And during a flash sale we've seen updates peak at roughly three thousand a second.

speaker: Olumide
text: Honestly the quickest win would be dual writes. Whenever the catalog service writes to MySQL, it also writes the document to Elasticsearch. Done.

speaker: Wei
text: The catalog service isn't the only writer though. I counted last quarter, fourteen different services write to the catalog tables directly. Pricing, the merchant importer, the promotions engine...

speaker: Sofia
text: And if the MySQL write succeeds and the Elasticsearch write times out, which one wins? You end up with an index that drifts and no way to replay what you missed.

speaker: Wei
text: And retrying from fourteen services means fourteen different retry implementations.

speaker: Grace
text: Yeah, I think dual writes are off the table. Too many writers, and no way to recover when the two stores disagree.

speaker: Wei
text: The obvious alternative is change data capture. Debezium reads the MySQL binlog and publishes every row change to Kafka. It doesn't matter who wrote the row.

speaker: Sofia
text: We already run Kafka on MSK for the order events, so that part's not new infrastructure.

speaker: Grace
text: Good. So we're going with Debezium on the catalog MySQL into Kafka, covering products, prices and stock levels.

speaker: Wei
text: Then something has to turn row changes into search documents. I'd use Flink for that, it's what everyone uses for streaming.

speaker: Olumide
text: Flink's fine by me.

speaker: Grace
text: OK, Flink for the stream processing then.

speaker: Olumide
text: One wrinkle. A search document needs the full category path and the brand name, but the change events only carry IDs. I'd put a Redis cache in front of the category and brand lookups so we're not hammering MySQL for every event.

speaker: Wei
text: Makes sense.

speaker: Grace
text: OK, add the Redis cache for the lookups.

speaker: Sofia
text: Kafka side, I'd start the catalog topics at twelve partitions, keyed by product ID so all the changes for one product stay in order.

speaker: Wei
text: Twelve is fine to start.

speaker: Hamid
text: Ooh, while we're streaming price changes anyway, could we feed them into the app for price-drop alerts? Like, notify people who wishlisted something?

speaker: Sofia
text: Wait, actually, I need to flag something about stock before we go further.

speaker: Sofia
text: Stock isn't really owned by the catalog database. The warehouse system is the source of truth, and a sync job copies stock levels into catalog MySQL every ten minutes. So CDC on that table still gives us ten-minute-old stock.

speaker: Hamid
text: That kills the one-minute target for stock.

speaker: Grace
text: OK, then let's narrow it. CDC on the catalog MySQL covers products and prices. Stock has to come from somewhere closer to the warehouse system, and where exactly is an open question for now.

speaker: Olumide
text: Let me poke at what the warehouse team already publishes. I think they have some kind of event stream for the fulfilment side.

speaker: Wei
text: Back to sizing. Three thousand updates a second at peak, and an Elasticsearch bulk request realistically does maybe a hundred and fifty documents a second per consumer once you include enrichment.

speaker: Sofia
text: So twelve partitions caps us at about eighteen hundred a second. We need at least twenty consumers at peak.

speaker: Wei
text: And you can't add partitions later without reshuffling the keys, which breaks per-product ordering. I'd go straight to thirty-two.

speaker: Grace
text: OK, thirty-two partitions instead of twelve. That gives us headroom for the next sale.

speaker: Olumide
text: How often do we flush bulk requests to Elasticsearch?

speaker: Wei
text: I'd say every five seconds or a thousand documents, whichever comes first. But I haven't load tested it.

speaker: Grace
text: Let's take five seconds or a thousand docs for now and revisit after the load test.

speaker: Olumide
text: Something we haven't talked about: full reindexes. When we change the mapping, or something goes wrong, we need to rebuild the whole index from scratch.

speaker: Wei
text: I'd keep the nightly Airflow job, but run it weekly as a safety net that rebuilds into a fresh index and swaps the alias.

speaker: Olumide
text: That's two code paths building documents. They'll drift. I'd rather replay from Kafka: compacted topics, reset the consumer offsets, rebuild into a new index.

speaker: Sofia
text: Compacted topics holding forty million products is a lot of storage on MSK, and a full replay at our throughput is hours anyway.

speaker: Olumide
text: Until the two paths produce different documents and nobody notices for a month.

speaker: Grace
text: We're going in circles on this one, and we don't need the answer for the first milestone. Let's leave the reindex strategy open. Wei, can you write up both options with a rough storage and runtime cost for each?

speaker: Wei
text: Yep, will do.

speaker: Sofia
text: Can I go back to Flink? I've been chewing on it. Who's on call for it? Nobody on my team has ever run Flink. Checkpoints, savepoints, upgrades, the JobManager falling over at three in the morning.

speaker: Wei
text: Fair. And looking at what we actually need, it's stateless. Each change event becomes one document update plus a couple of lookups. There are no windows, no joins between streams.

speaker: Wei
text: A plain Kafka consumer service would do it. Call it the indexer, written in Go, scaled by running more instances up to the partition count.

speaker: Olumide
text: I'd be happier with that. I can actually debug a Go service.

speaker: Grace
text: OK, let's reverse the Flink decision. We use a plain indexer service consuming from Kafka. Flink is out because nobody can operate it and the job doesn't need state.

speaker: Olumide
text: And if the indexer is a long-running service, then I don't think we need Redis either. The category tree is about twenty thousand nodes and brands are around fifty thousand rows. That fits in memory easily.

speaker: Wei
text: Load them at startup, and keep them fresh from the category and brand changes on the same CDC stream.

speaker: Sofia
text: Please. One less thing to page me about.

speaker: Grace
text: OK, drop Redis. The indexer keeps the category and brand lookups in memory and refreshes them from CDC.

speaker: Hamid
text: From my side, what do we show if the indexer falls behind? Can we at least alert on it?

speaker: Sofia
text: We alert on consumer lag. If the oldest unprocessed event is more than sixty seconds old, that's a page, because at that point we're missing Hamid's one-minute target.

speaker: Grace
text: Agreed, page on consumer lag over sixty seconds.

speaker: Grace
text: Let's wrap with owners. Wei, Debezium?

speaker: Wei
text: I'll have the Debezium connector running against the staging replica by December 4th.

speaker: Olumide
text: I'll start the indexer skeleton this week, and I'll come back on the warehouse events thing.

speaker: Sofia
text: I'll set up the topics on MSK once the partition count is final, which I guess it is now.

speaker: Grace
text: It is. Thanks all. Wei, go sleep.
